messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus is a seventy-one-year-old retired insurance agent, single, who presented to the clinic with a PCL-5 score of 39, indicating moderate PTSD symptoms that have persisted for decades. His trauma originates in childhood physical abuse perpetrated by his father, a man who drank heavily and became unpredictably violent. Marcus recalls being struck with a belt, pushed against walls, and threatened with worse if he made a sound or told anyone. The violence was often preceded by the smell of whiskey on his father's breath—a sensory signature that became fused with terror and helplessness. His mother, whom he had depended on for protection, ultimately did nothing to stop it. By adolescence Marcus had learned to make himself small, to anticipate danger in every raised voice, and to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that those closest to him could not be trusted.

For decades Marcus functioned adequately. He built a career in insurance, maintained a professional demeanor, and lived alone—a choice that felt safer than the vulnerability of partnership. But in his late sixties, as he moved toward retirement, the symptoms that had always simmered beneath the surface began to intensify. The traumatic memories themselves became intrusive and vivid, appearing without warning as sudden fragments—a flash of his father's face, the sensation of impact, the acrid smell of alcohol—that felt more real and immediate than his ordinary recollections. These fragments would arrive unbidden while he was at his desk or driving home, and they would grip him with the same terror he had felt as a child. When he encountered the smell of alcohol in public—a colleague's breath after lunch, a stranger in the grocery store—the memories became overwhelming, and his body would flood with panic as if the danger were happening in the present moment.

The intrusive memories and their sensory vividness deepened Marcus's conviction that something was fundamentally wrong with him and his body. He had come to believe that his own physiology was a betrayer—his racing heart, his shallow breathing, his hypervigilance were proof that danger was real, even when his rational mind knew he was safe at home. This sense of bodily betrayal fed a growing preoccupation with threat. He began to listen intently for sounds in his apartment—a footstep in the hallway, a door closing, the creak of the building settling—and he interpreted these ordinary noises as potential intrusions. He felt threatened by strangers approaching him even in benign situations, like a cashier handing him change or a neighbor greeting him in the lobby. His vigilance was exhausting, and it was also utterly convincing; his body's alarm responses felt like evidence that danger was everywhere.

The more Marcus's threat system activated, the more his memories intruded. Each moment of panic seemed to pull up new fragments of the trauma, and each memory fragment triggered a fresh wave of threat perception. To manage the unbearable cycle, he developed rituals and mental strategies. He began to perform small mental acts—counting in patterns, repeating phrases—as if these rituals could prevent something terrible from happening again. He kept his mind occupied constantly, filling every gap with work, podcasts, or mental tasks, anything to prevent the memories from surfacing. He avoided television and news, refusing to watch anything that resembled violence or family conflict. These strategies provided temporary relief, but they also reinforced his core belief that he was in danger and that only constant vigilance and these private rituals could keep him safe.

The avoidance and magical thinking, however, deepened his sense that the threat was real and that his body's reactions were justified. His rituals seemed to work in the moment—nothing bad happened—and this apparent success convinced him that the danger was genuine and that his strategies were necessary. He began to avoid social situations more broadly, declining invitations to retirement parties or client gatherings. The thought of talking to strangers, of making small talk, triggered memories of his father's unpredictable mood shifts and the fear of saying something wrong. Interactions that should have been routine—a conversation with a barista, a phone call from an old colleague—became sources of dread. His isolation deepened, and with it, his conviction that people could not be trusted and that safety lay only in solitude and control.

By the time Marcus sought help, he had become almost entirely confined by his symptoms. He had retired early from his career because the office environment had become intolerable—too many strangers, too many unexpected interactions. He spent most of his time at home, performing his rituals, keeping his mind occupied, avoiding anything that might trigger a memory. He was certain that the people responsible for his suffering—his father, his mother—had never faced consequences for what they had done, and this unfairness gnawed at him. What brought him finally to the clinic was a moment of clarity: he realized he was no longer living, only managing to survive. He hoped that treatment might help him reclaim some part of his life, though he was deeply afraid that his body would never stop betraying him, and that the danger he felt so acutely might be permanent.

violation_explanations: Triggers (smell of alcohol, sounds in apartment, strangers) appear throughout the vignette, and negative appraisals (bodily betrayal, danger is real, people cannot be trusted) are present, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that encountering triggers drives or leads to the formation of negative appraisals—the causal relationship is absent.

While negative appraisals (threat is real, danger is everywhere) and triggers (alcohol smell, noises, strangers) both appear, no paragraph demonstrates that Marcus's negative beliefs cause him to perceive new triggers or interpret stimuli as triggering—the reverse causal direction is not established.

Marcus's maladaptive strategies (rituals, mental counting, avoidance, constant mental occupation) are clearly described, and negative appraisals (danger is real, body is a betrayer) are present, but no paragraph conveys that his strategies drive or reinforce new negative appraisals—the causal link is missing.

Marcus's maladaptive strategies (rituals, avoidance, mental occupation) are described as providing temporary relief and seeming to work, which he interprets as evidence of danger; however, no paragraph explicitly states that these strategies themselves cause or intensify his sense of threat—the causal relationship is not clearly established.
